definition: A theoretical result stating that no single machine learning algorithm performs best across all possible problems; performance depends on how well an algorithm's assumptions match the specific problem.
details: The no free lunch theorem is a foundational concept in ML theory, cautioning against the notion of a universally 'best' algorithm and emphasizing that model and algorithm choice should be informed by the structure of the specific problem at hand.

explainer.lead: The No Free Lunch Theorem states that no single machine learning algorithm performs best across all possible problems. It matters because it warns against believing any algorithm is universally superior and ties performance to how well an algorithm's assumptions fit the problem.

tiers.eli5: No single recipe is best for every dish — which one wins depends on what you're cooking.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to justify choosing models and algorithms based on the structure of the specific problem at hand. A pitfall is picking an algorithm by reputation alone instead of matching its assumptions to the task.
tiers.paperLevel: A theoretical result: averaged across all possible problems, no algorithm outperforms another, so performance depends on the match between the algorithm's assumptions and the specific problem.

explainer.example: A model that excels on one dataset may underperform on an unrelated one, so a practitioner compares candidates on the actual problem rather than assuming a single winner.
